en: XIV. The Chapter on the Yoginīs of the Pīṭhas and Other Sites Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret, the supreme confluence of the pīṭhas; through the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, there arises a state of unified equal flavor.
The wheel of non-dual equality, together with the three colors, is the city; within the square mandala, however, is the supreme twenty-four-spoked wheel.
In its center is a magnificent great lotus with petals of every color, endowed with eight petals and a pericarp, and adorned with filaments.
It has four gates and eight pillars, beautifully adorned with archways; it is decorated with strings of pearls and half-strings of pearls, and is endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
In the center of the solar disk, one should visualize Vajrasattva, the Great Bliss, who has become liquefied from the vowels and consonants and consists of the five gnoses.
Having transformed that, one should visualize him as Heruka, the True Vajra, the supreme destroyer at the time of the great dissolution, who rends all those who are difficult to subdue.
Bhairava and Kālarātri are made into the soles of his feet; his face is formidable with fangs, he has three eyes, and he is terrifyingly fearsome.
His body has a blue-tipped form, and his body is ablaze with blue flames; he wears a crown of garlands of skulls and is empowered by the five Buddhas.
He wears a crown of universal vajras adorned with a crescent moon; he has six faces, displaying the heroic, the loathsome, the erotic with laughter, the wrathful, and the graceful expressions.
The body is sealed with the six mudrās, adorned with various ornaments, entered into union with Vārāhī, and well-encircled by her two knees.
She stands in the posture of *pratyālīḍha*, with her body positioned in the *ālīḍha* stance; she is terrifying, uttering cries of "hā hā," "saḥ," "hūṃ," and "hī hī."
One should utter the sounds *hūṃ hūṃ*, *saṃ haṃ*, and *aṭṭaṭṭa*. [The colors are] blue, yellow, red, green, and white.
With his face turned upward, most fierce, and possessing a black serpent from the sky as his neck-ornament; he is joined with the vajra and bell, and is pressed against the breasts of the goddess.

He wears a garment of Rudra’s hide, with half his body smeared with flowing blood; he holds a skull, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, a curved knife, a goad, a noose, and a severed head, as well as a mallet and a ḍamaru drum. He is fierce, adorned on his forehead with a spear and a flaming mudrā.
One should visualize such a mudrā, naked with disheveled hair, possessing the same color, arms, and posture [as the deity], and adorned with a girdle of bone fragments.
The consort Vārāhī should be conceived in this way, free from the delusions of the yoginīs, absorbed in wisdom and means, and possessing the true bliss of compassionate passion.
Born from the cause of the welfare of sentient beings, with a mind moistened by compassion, they enjoy the vast expanse of space and are eager for the essence of great compassion.

She is to be purified within the existence of the six realms of rebirth, and is intent upon accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings; she is born from the wisdom of emptiness, free from conceptual construction, and without abode.
Devoid of intrinsic nature, supreme, subtle, and free from bindu and nāda—having perceived the equality of the commitment (samaya), they are most excellent both externally and internally.
In the heart, within the center of a moon mandala, is the Wisdom Samaya; having visualized it with its respective color, arms, and weapons, one should see the seed-syllable of the Moon-Vajra.
Having meditated upon that very [deity] in the heart, one should perform the yoga of service; one should then perform the placement of the *ḍākinīs* in the lotus according to the proper sequence.
In the east is the placement of Ḍākinī, and likewise Lāmā in the north; Khaṇḍarohā is in the west, and likewise Rūpiṇī in the south.
They are of four kinds—blue, green, red, and yellow; they have three eyes, distorted faces, are fierce, with disheveled hair, and are naked.
Complete with all ornaments and sealed with the five mudrās, they hold a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff resting upon their left shoulders.
A hand-drum and a curved knife, a severed head, and the supreme *samaya* of the *ḍākinīs*; skull-cups filled with the water of *bodhicitta* rest upon the vases.
One should perform the placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa), beginning with the Svādhiṣṭhāna, according to the sequence established by the ancients.
In the northeast, at Pullīramalaya, the consort of Khaṇḍakapālin is Pracaṇḍā, who is sky-blue in color.
In Jālandhara is Mahākaṅkāla-Caṇḍākṣī, who is yellow; in Oḍiyāna is Kaṅkālaprabhāvatī, who is green.
Arbude, Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrinī, Mahānāsā, and Gaganagaurā.
At Godāvarī, Vīramatī was drunk by the enemy of the gods (Śiva); at Rāmeśvara, Haritā was Amitābha’s Kharvarī.
In Devīkoṭa is Vajraprabhā Laṅkeśvarī, who is as white as the sky.
In Mālava, Vajradehadrumacchāyā is yellow; in Kāmarūpa, Aṅkurikā and Airāvatī are green.
In Oḍra, Vajrajaṭilamahābhairavā is sky-blue; in Triśakuni, Mahāvīravāyuvegā is yellow.
In Kośalā, Vajrahūṃkāra and Surābhakṣī are green; in Kaliṅga, Subhadra and Śyāmādevī are sky-blue.
In Lampāka, Vajrabhadra and Subhadrā are yellow; in Kāñcī, Mahābhairava and Hayakarṇā are green.
In the Himalayas, Virūpākṣa and Khagānanā are sky-blue; in Pretapurī, Mahābala and Cakravega are yellow.
At the household deity is Ratnavajra Khaṇḍarohā, who is green; in Saurāṣṭra is Hayagrīva Sauṇḍinī, who is as white as the sky.
In Suvarṇadvīpa, Ākāśagarbha and Cakravarmiṇī are yellow. In the city, Śrī Heruka and Suvīrā are green.
Alternatively, one may perform the visualization according to one's preference by means of the distinctions of body, speech, and mind; and at the gates, in due order, starting from the left.
In the east is Kākāsyā, in the north Ulūkāsyā; in the west Śvānāsyā, and in the south Śūkarāsyā, who are blue, red, green, and yellow respectively.
In the southeast is Yamadāḍhī, red; in the southwest is Yamadūtī, blue; in the northwest is Yamadaṃṣṭrī, smoky grey.
In the northeast is Yamamathanī, white and pale yellow.
The heroes Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, together with Pracaṇḍā and the rest, have one face and four arms; they stand in the ālīḍha posture.
Wearing garlands of skulls and garments of tiger skin, bearing the five mudrās, they firmly embrace the feet of the Goddess; they are naked and adorned with garlands of severed heads.

Three-eyed and adorned on the forehead with a vajra garland, they are engaged in the non-dual yoga through the embrace of the vajra-bell; the goddesses press against their breasts. Their hands hold a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a ḍamaru drum. Alternatively, according to the division of the three families, they bear as their primary emblems the vajra, the wheel, and the lotus.
